rewrites.summary:
Trans visitors face grave danger here, with a hard internal split: in the West Bank, same-sex conduct is not criminalised (Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual-private-sex offences, carried into the 1960 penal code applied there), but there are no protections, family/clan hostility is severe, and the Palestinian Authority has not legislated or signed key treaties. In the other part, Gaza, a 1936 British Mandate code technically allows up to 10 years for consensual same-sex acts, Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality, and the area is in a catastrophic war.

Trans identities are nowhere explicitly criminalised, but public-morality provisions can catch trans people, gender-affirming healthcare is essentially destroyed or unavailable, police action against a queer organisation drew rights-group condemnation, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context colours but does not set the assessment: Israeli courts now grant asylum claims from LGBT Palestinians who flee the territories — litigation flux in a neighbouring jurisdiction, and the strongest available signal of how little local protection exists. A 'pinkwashing' critique that the occupying power exploits queer and trans Palestinian suffering to legitimise itself is noted in several sources; the safety picture cannot be separated from the wider political situation.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The destroyed or unavailable gender-affirming healthcare and the family/clan hostility dynamics describe the situation of residents, not the legal framework alone. The asylum-flight pattern to neighbouring Israel is a resident phenomenon: nearly a hundred LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.

A human-rights monitoring organisation and a local legal-aid centre interviewed 12 Palestinian women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer and documented widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; the regional activist movement — personal stories, cross-border alliances and national campaigns — is resident life, not visitor guidance.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The two parts — West Bank and Gaza — are scored as one de jure unit, yet Gaza is far worse in practice because of the war and Hamas, the group controlling the area. No source covers border screening, document handling or passport-marker practice for trans visitors, and no marriage or partner-travel recognition fact for trans visitors is recorded anywhere in the sources. Reported Hamas executions for alleged homosexuality and the police clampdown are documented claims, not independently verified elsewhere.

blindSourceSummaries: A country page of an advocacy organisation: the two parts of the nation run under different penal codes — the code inherited from the historic administration, dated 1936, is still in force in one part and is silent on trans identities, but trans people can be caught by public-morality provisions; a critique warns that the occupation marginalises queer and trans people alongside everyone else; de facto oppression is documented.

A legal-information page: the criminal law in one part derives from a 1960 penal code that carried forward a 1951 revision which dropped consensual-private-sex offences; practical reality is harsher than formal law because of social and family persecution.

A community encyclopedia entry: decriminalisation is a patchwork — the historic-era code applied in one region until 1951, a later code without any same-sex prohibition applied in the other part, and the neighbouring nation stopped using that code in 1977; the national authority has not legislated, there is no explicit prohibition on trans identity, periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported, and the national authority has not signed key treaties.

A report of a monitoring organisation (16 Apr 2018): LGBT people across the wider region are finding ways to speak out — personal stories, cross-border alliances, and national and regional movements combatting homophobia and transphobia; regional movement context for local LGBT life.

A news report: rights groups condemned the police for banning LGBTQ activity — after police action against a queer organisation, the organisation received a wave of hate messages that activists called a serious threat to the gay community.

A report of a monitoring organisation (11 Jun 2018) prepared with a local legal-aid centre: women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer were interviewed and reported widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; a historic-era code provision punishing consensual same-sex acts by up to 10 years, and the 1960 code used in the other part, were analysed as violating privacy and non-discrimination.

A news report: the neighbouring nation will allow LGBT people granted temporary asylum to work — nearly a hundred LGBT people have received temporary permits to seek refuge there after fleeing violence in the nation.
rewrites.notes: Four-field split of country:PSE (who hard-required as country:PSE regardless of record naming) from current_summary plus the seven source claims. Visitor risk (legal protections/enforcement, practical safety; no documents/screening or marriage/partner-travel facts on record — moved to outOfScope) in summary: West Bank legality-without-protection, Gaza 10-year historic-era code with reported executions and catastrophic war, trans identities not explicitly criminalised but caught by public-morality provisions, destroyed/unavailable gender-affirming care (echoed from current_localsOnly), police clampdown on a queer organisation with rights-group condemnation, periodic transphobic threats/attacks, non-signatory status. Courts of the neighbouring nation granting asylum claims to LGBT Palestinians (litigation flux) and the pinkwashing/occupation critique to tangentialFactors. Resident-facing: destroyed care, family/clan hostility dynamics, asylum-flight with 'nearly a hundred' temporary permits, 12-woman interview findings, and regional resident activism to localsOnly. One de jure unit vs far-worse-in-practice split (current_outOfScope preserved and expanded), no border-screening/document/passport-marker or marriage/partner-travel source, and unverified-execution caveat to outOfScopeNotes. Blind mirrors substitution-only per rules 7/7e: names, demonyms, institutions, region names, directions, bill numbers, and the exact 90/12 counts generalised; apostrophes avoided to keep stems gate-safe.
